bill.title: Providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Bureau of Land Management relating to "National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska Integrated Activity Plan Record of Decision".
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
bill.officialSummary: This joint resolution nullifies the rule submitted by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) titled National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska Integrated Activity Plan Record of Decision and issued on April 25, 2022. BLM's plan provides for the management of the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska, which is an approximately 23-million-acre area on Alaska’s North Slope. The 2022 plan replaced the 2020 plan and closed approximately 48% of the reserve to oil and gas leasing in order to protect certain surface resources and uses, such as protecting wildlife and providing subsistence for communities. Thus, the joint resolution removes the protections provided under the 2022 plan and reverts to the 2020 plan.

classification.plainSummary: This resolution would cancel a 2022 federal land-management plan for the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska and restore the previous 2020 plan. The 2022 plan closed roughly half of the 23-million-acre reserve to oil and gas leasing to protect wildlife and subsistence uses. Reversing it would reopen those areas to energy development under the earlier rules.

industries.rationale: The resolution would reopen approximately 48% of the National Petroleum Reserve to oil and gas leasing, directly expanding access for extraction companies.
Environmental and conservation organizations have a direct stake in the wildlife and subsistence protections that would be removed by reverting to the 2020 plan.

plain.whatItDoes: This joint resolution would cancel the rule submitted by the federal land agency titled National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska Integrated Activity Plan Record of Decision and issued on April 25, 2022.
plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who buys fuel or heats a home. People who live near a mine, and people who work in one.
plain.everydayEffect: If it passed, the change would show up in what fuel costs. Nothing has changed yet. Most bills never become law.

method.formula: score = Σ_industries ( donorShare(industry) × billWeight(industry) ), where billWeight = classifierConfidence / Σ classifierConfidence. Range 0–1, read as a weighted share of disclosed itemized money.

ordinary.text: They wrote this bill. Sponsoring a bill about your own district's industry is the ordinary case, not the odd one.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
